issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette:
Kwame Mensah, a 72-year-old Coast Guard serviceman who had spent decades trusting routine and procedure, traced the beginning of his difficulties to a chemical exposure during a harbor response call. A storage container on the dock had ruptured, and he was among the first to move in. He remembered the strange, almost wrong stillness just before people started shouting—a pocket of silence over the water, no gulls, no machinery he could make out, only the sight of a pale vapor spreading low across the pier. He could still see it in frozen images: the sheen on the metal railing, a crewman bent over coughing, the mask on another responder not seated properly against his face. At the time he kept moving, but later the scene returned to him not as an ordinary recollection but like a film that restarted without his permission, or as sharp photographic flashes that left him shaken.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found that when the memory came back, it hit with so much force that he had to stop whatever he was doing. He would be standing in his kitchen or checking equipment at work and suddenly feel flooded by the same dread and bodily jolt, as if he were back on the dock. Those returns of the scene convinced him that he was no longer able to handle strain the way he once had. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about the exposure at all, he would be overwhelmed beyond control. The more vividly the event replayed, the more certain he became that even a slight upset could undo him and that the world itself was fundamentally unsafe.

That shift in what he believed about himself and the world fed directly into how he moved through ordinary life. Because he was convinced danger could emerge without warning and that he would not cope if it did, he stayed on guard even at home, scanning for signs that something was off. What frightened him most was silence. A quiet room, the television turned off, the pause before his wife answered from another room—these moments felt loaded, like the breathless stillness on the dock before the seriousness of the leak became clear. He would feel his chest tighten and his body surge into readiness, as though unusual silence itself meant something harmful was about to happen.

The same thing happened on duty. In the Coast Guard station, if a corridor went unexpectedly quiet or the usual hum of radios dropped out, Kwame’s body reacted before he could think. He would feel his heart pound, his hands tense, and the dock scene would begin to unspool again in his mind. A moment of silence could call up the visual fragments so vividly that he had to step away. In that sense the memories and the sense of threat had become tightly bound: the mental replay made him feel endangered in the present, and feeling endangered made the images return with even greater force.

Over months, he tried to manage this by keeping his mind away from the exposure. He avoided dwelling on that day because he was certain that if he let the memory in, he would not be able to handle what followed. Yet the constant watchfulness seemed to trap him with the event rather than distance him from it. When he sat at home alert to every pause in the house, or when his body reacted to a sudden hush at work, he found himself right back with those photographic snapshots of vapor on the pier and men struggling to breathe. Each episode left him more persuaded that his reactions were proof of diminished resilience. He would tell himself that if a quiet room could unravel him, then he truly could not cope with even minor stress.

His marriage had narrowed around this pattern. Even inside his own home, he rarely relaxed, and his wife had begun keeping noise on in the background because she could see how quickly silence changed him. At work, he still reported for duty, but he positioned himself where activity was constant and found excuses to avoid quieter areas near the docks. These habits made sense to him because he believed the world was dangerous and that staying alert was the only thing preventing another catastrophe, but they also kept his body primed and his mind close to the worst moments of the exposure.

Kwame finally agreed to seek help after an episode at home when the house fell completely quiet during a brief power outage. The silence brought an immediate rush of heat, a pounding heart, and the full visual replay of the dock, so overwhelming that he had to sit down and could not speak for several minutes. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the conclusion he drew from it: that he was becoming unable to manage ordinary life, even in his own home. He came in hoping for some way to stop living as if danger were always about to break through the next silent moment.
